sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Echo and Chi are the two most common Gin alternatives in Go job postings, and they represent two distinct philosophies worth understanding. Echo provides a richer built-in API — custom context, flexible binder, interface-based validation — and is popular in teams that want Gin-like ergonomics with more extensibility. Chi takes the opposite approach: pure stdlib compatibility, zero allocations, and the ability to reuse any net/http middleware ever written. Knowing when and why to choose between them demonstrates architectural judgment beyond "what does the team already use".

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Echo uses a custom `echo.Context` interface that wraps request and response with convenience methods; you can extend it with your own context type carrying application dependencies. Echo's binder is interface-based (`echo.Binder`) so you can plug in custom binding logic per content type. Chi's defining characteristic is that every handler is a plain `http.Handler` and every middleware is a standard `func(http.Handler) http.Handler` — there is no framework-specific function type. This means Chi is not a framework in the traditional sense; it's a router that works entirely within the stdlib HTTP contract.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Echo context and routing**: `e.GET`, `e.Group`, named params `/:id`; `c.Param`, `c.QueryParam`, `c.Bind`, `c.JSON`, `c.String`.
- **Echo middleware**: `e.Use(middleware.Logger())`, group-level and route-level middleware; `echo.WrapMiddleware` converts stdlib middleware to Echo middleware.
- **Echo binder/validator interface**: implement `echo.Validator` with `Validate(i interface{}) error`; registered via `e.Validator = &CustomValidator{}`.
- **Chi router**: `chi.NewRouter()`, `r.Get/Post/Put/Delete`, URL params via `chi.URLParam(r, "id")`; `r.Route` for sub-routers.
- **Chi middleware stack**: `r.Use(middleware.Logger, middleware.Recoverer)` — all standard `func(http.Handler) http.Handler` functions.
- **Chi's stdlib compatibility advantage**: any net/http-compatible middleware (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, JWT libraries) works directly with Chi without adapters.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Chi handlers work with ANY net/http middleware**: this is the key advantage over Gin and Echo — the entire Go middleware ecosystem (from 2013 to today) is directly compatible.
- **Echo's binder is more flexible than Gin's**: Echo can bind from JSON, form, query, path, and headers in a single call, and you can implement a custom binder for exotic formats.
- **When to choose Chi**: when you need to integrate many third-party middleware packages (observability, auth, rate limiting) from the stdlib ecosystem without wrapper adapters.
- **When to choose Echo**: when you want richer built-in features (binder, validator, renderer) and are building a cohesive team codebase that doesn't need to mix many external middleware libraries.
- **URL param access difference**: Gin uses `c.Param("id")`; Chi uses `chi.URLParam(r, "id")`; Echo uses `c.Param("id")` — a surface-level detail that trips up candidates switching frameworks.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "I choose Chi when stdlib middleware compatibility matters — if I'm integrating OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, or third-party JWT middleware that ships as standard net/http middleware, Chi lets me plug them in directly without any wrapper code. Every Chi handler is a plain http.Handler, so the team can bring in any middleware ever written for Go's stdlib HTTP without adapter layers. I choose Echo when I want a richer built-in API — particularly its flexible binder that handles JSON, query params, and path params in one call, and its interface-based validator that integrates cleanly with go-playground/validator. For most greenfield projects I default to Chi because stdlib compatibility compounds over time as the dependency graph grows."
